Personally I'd recommend looking at Qt-based projects as a good place to start. It's a really nice ecosystem that tends to encourage well-designed projects, and there are a ton to choose from, including the entirety of KDE.

Some people will point out that Qt isn't totally standard C++, and they're right: Qt added support for some thing like RAII-managed mutexes and smart pointers before these were available in the C++ standard, so now we have things like QSharedPointer vs. shared_ptr, etc. Likewise it provides a language-level signal/slot mechanism which, while really nice, is also non-standard C++. So that can be a disadvantage from a certain perspective.

Still, I find Qt a joy to work with, and using it doesn't appear to have damaged by ability to go back to standard C++11/14. It's also extremely practical (I've used it professionally) and comes with a surprisingly high-quality free IDE called Qt Creator.

Wikipedia has a list of projects using Qt; many of these are open source.
